title: "Week 17 Self-Assessment"
subtitle: "Research Credibility, p-Hacking, and Replication"
---



## Instructions

Test your understanding of research credibility, questionable research practices, and the replication crisis. Understanding these issues is essential for becoming a critical consumer of psychological research.

---

## Part 1: Conceptual Questions

### Question 1: The Replication Crisis

The "replication crisis" refers to:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Too many studies being published</option><option value='answer'>Many published findings failing to replicate in subsequent studies</option><option value=''>Researchers copying each other's work</option><option value=''>Difficulty recruiting participants</option></select>

A famous replication project in psychology found that approximately what percentage of original findings replicated?

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Over 90%</option><option value=''>About 75%</option><option value='answer'>About 36-40%</option><option value=''>Less than 10%</option></select>

### Question 2: Why Does Replication Matter?

Replication is important because:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>It shows researchers can copy each other</option><option value='answer'>It helps us distinguish genuine effects from statistical flukes or methodological artifacts</option><option value=''>It increases the number of publications</option><option value=''>It is required by ethics committees</option></select>

If a finding does NOT replicate, this suggests:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>The original researchers cheated</option><option value='answer'>The original finding may have been a false positive, or there may be important moderating factors</option><option value=''>Science is broken</option><option value=''>We should never trust any research</option></select>

### Question 3: p-Hacking

p-Hacking refers to:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Breaking into statistical software</option><option value='answer'>Manipulating data or analyses to achieve p < .05</option><option value=''>Using very small p-values</option><option value=''>Reporting exact p-values</option></select>

Which of the following is an example of p-hacking?

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Pre-registering your analysis plan</option><option value='answer'>Running multiple analyses and only reporting the significant ones</option><option value=''>Using a large sample size</option><option value=''>Reporting effect sizes</option></select>

### Question 4: More p-Hacking Examples

Which is a questionable research practice?

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Deciding your sample size before collecting data</option><option value='answer'>Stopping data collection as soon as you get p < .05</option><option value=''>Reporting all your analyses, significant or not</option><option value=''>Using pre-registered hypotheses</option></select>

Selectively removing outliers until your result becomes significant is:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Good data cleaning</option><option value=''>Standard practice</option><option value='answer'>A form of p-hacking</option><option value=''>Always necessary</option></select>

### Question 5: HARKing

HARKing stands for:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>High Achievement Research Knowledge</option><option value='answer'>Hypothesising After Results are Known</option><option value=''>Honest And Reliable Knowledge</option><option value=''>Helpful Analyses for Research Knowledge</option></select>

HARKing is problematic because:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>It takes too long</option><option value='answer'>It presents exploratory findings as if they were predicted, inflating false positive rates</option><option value=''>It requires too many participants</option><option value=''>Hypotheses are unnecessary</option></select>

### Question 6: Publication Bias

Publication bias means:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>All studies get published equally</option><option value='answer'>Studies with significant results are more likely to be published than non-significant ones</option><option value=''>Journals are biased against psychology</option><option value=''>Too many studies are published</option></select>

Publication bias contributes to the replication crisis because:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>It encourages more research</option><option value='answer'>The published literature over-represents findings that may be false positives</option><option value=''>It makes journals too selective</option><option value=''>Non-significant results are always wrong</option></select>

---

## Part 2: Interpretation Questions

### Question 7: Identifying Questionable Practices

A researcher reports: "After extensive data analysis, we discovered an unexpected but significant relationship between X and Y."

What concern does this raise?

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>The finding is definitely wrong</option><option value='answer'>Possible HARKing - the finding may be exploratory but presented as if predicted</option><option value=''>The analysis was too extensive</option><option value=''>The relationship is too strong</option></select>

### Question 8: Evaluating Research Practices

Which researcher is following best practices?

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Researcher A: Removes outliers until getting p < .05</option><option value=''>Researcher B: Only reports significant findings from many analyses</option><option value='answer'>Researcher C: Pre-registered hypothesis and reports all results regardless of significance</option><option value=''>Researcher D: Changes hypothesis after seeing preliminary data</option></select>

### Question 9: The "File Drawer Problem"

The "file drawer problem" refers to:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Researchers losing their data</option><option value='answer'>Non-significant studies remaining unpublished (in file drawers) while significant ones get published</option><option value=''>Too much data storage needed</option><option value=''>Poor file organisation</option></select>

This contributes to:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Better science</option><option value='answer'>A biased view of what effects actually exist</option><option value=''>Faster publication</option><option value=''>More efficient research</option></select>

### Question 10: Statistical Power

Low statistical power increases the risk of:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Finding an effect when none exists</option><option value='answer'>Missing a real effect (false negative) AND inflated effect sizes when effects are found</option><option value=''>Too many significant results</option><option value=''>Ethical violations</option></select>

Studies with low power that do find significant effects often:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Are more reliable</option><option value='answer'>Report inflated effect sizes (winner's curse)</option><option value=''>Have smaller p-values</option><option value=''>Are more likely to replicate</option></select>

---

## Part 3: Application Questions

### Question 11: Improving Research Credibility

Pre-registration helps prevent:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Data collection errors</option><option value='answer'>HARKing and p-hacking by committing to analyses before seeing data</option><option value=''>Participant dropout</option><option value=''>Plagiarism</option></select>

Open data and open materials help by:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Making research faster</option><option value='answer'>Allowing others to verify findings and detect errors</option><option value=''>Reducing costs</option><option value=''>Guaranteeing replication</option></select>

### Question 12: Evaluating Claims

A study claims to have found a significant effect (p = .049) after testing 20 different hypotheses.

Your main concern should be:

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>The effect is very strong</option><option value=''>The sample was too large</option><option value='answer'>Multiple comparisons increase the chance of a false positive - one in 20 tests would be 'significant' by chance</option><option value=''>The p-value is too small</option></select>

### Question 13: What Makes Research More Credible?

Which features increase your confidence in a finding?

Pre-registered hypothesis and analysis plan: <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>TRUE</option><option value=''>FALSE</option></select>

Large sample size with adequate power: <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>TRUE</option><option value=''>FALSE</option></select>

Only significant results reported from many analyses: <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>TRUE</option><option value='answer'>FALSE</option></select>

Successful independent replication: <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>TRUE</option><option value=''>FALSE</option></select>

Hypothesis changed after seeing the data: <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>TRUE</option><option value='answer'>FALSE</option></select>

Effect size reported alongside p-value: <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>TRUE</option><option value=''>FALSE</option></select>

---

## Part 4: MCQ Exam Practice

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}

### Scenario 1: Evaluating a Study

A researcher tests whether a new teaching method improves exam scores. They collect data from 20 students but find p = .08. They then collect 10 more students, re-analyse, and now find p = .04. They report only the final analysis.

1. **What questionable practice is this?** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>HARKing</option><option value='answer'>Optional stopping / peeking at data</option><option value=''>Pre-registration</option><option value=''>Replication</option></select>

2. **Why is this problematic?** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>30 students is too few</option><option value='answer'>Adding participants until reaching significance inflates false positive rate</option><option value=''>The effect is too small</option><option value=''>They should have used more students initially</option></select>

3. **A better approach would be:** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Never collect more data</option><option value='answer'>Pre-register the sample size and stick to it</option><option value=''>Stop at 20 students</option><option value=''>Use a one-tailed test</option></select>

:::

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}

### Scenario 2: Interpreting Replication Failure

Study A (original, n=30) finds: d = 0.85, p = .02
Study B (replication, n=200) finds: d = 0.12, p = .31

1. **The replication found:** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>A stronger effect</option><option value=''>The same effect</option><option value='answer'>A much smaller, non-significant effect</option><option value=''>A negative effect</option></select>

2. **Which study's effect size is likely more accurate?** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Study A (original)</option><option value='answer'>Study B (larger sample, more precise)</option><option value=''>They are equally accurate</option><option value=''>Neither</option></select>

3. **The original study's large effect size may have been due to:** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Better methodology</option><option value='answer'>Winner's curse (inflated effects in underpowered significant findings)</option><option value=''>More careful data collection</option><option value=''>Superior participants</option></select>

4. **What should we conclude?** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>The original study was fraudulent</option><option value='answer'>The effect may be smaller than originally reported, or not reliable</option><option value=''>Replications are always wrong</option><option value=''>Never trust psychology research</option></select>

:::

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}

### Scenario 3: Identifying Best Practices

A researcher plans to test whether exercise improves mood. Before collecting any data, they:
- Register their hypothesis on OSF
- Specify they will collect exactly 100 participants
- State they will use a paired t-test
- Commit to reporting all results regardless of significance

1. **This is an example of:** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>HARKing</option><option value=''>p-hacking</option><option value='answer'>Pre-registration</option><option value=''>Publication bias</option></select>

2. **This practice helps prevent:** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Participant dropout</option><option value='answer'>Changing the analysis plan based on the data</option><option value=''>Recruitment difficulties</option><option value=''>Ethical violations</option></select>

3. **If the final p-value is .07, the researcher should:** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Collect more data until p < .05</option><option value=''>Change to a one-tailed test</option><option value='answer'>Report the non-significant result as planned</option><option value=''>Not publish the study</option></select>

4. **This researcher is demonstrating:** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Poor planning</option><option value='answer'>Commitment to transparency and reducing bias</option><option value=''>Unnecessary rigidity</option><option value=''>Overcaution</option></select>

:::

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}

### Scenario 4: Red Flags in Research

A published paper reports finding significant effects for 18 out of 20 tested relationships (all p < .05).

1. **Is this pattern suspicious?** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>TRUE</option><option value=''>FALSE</option></select>

2. **Why?** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>18 significant results is impossible</option><option value='answer'>This pattern is unlikely without selective reporting or p-hacking</option><option value=''>Too many relationships were tested</option><option value=''>The effects must be very large</option></select>

3. **What would increase your confidence in these findings?**
<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>If they reported even more significant results</option><option value='answer'>If the study was pre-registered and the analysis plan showed these specific tests were planned</option><option value=''>If the sample size was smaller</option><option value=''>If only significant results were discussed</option></select>

:::

---

## Summary Checklist

Before moving on, make sure you can:

- [ ] Explain what the replication crisis is and why it matters
- [ ] Define p-hacking and give examples
- [ ] Define HARKing and explain why it's problematic
- [ ] Explain publication bias and the file drawer problem
- [ ] Describe how pre-registration improves research credibility
- [ ] Identify red flags in research reporting
- [ ] Explain the relationship between statistical power and replication
- [ ] Describe what makes research findings more credible

::: {.callout-important}
## Becoming a Critical Consumer
Understanding these issues helps you evaluate research critically. When reading a study, ask: Was it pre-registered? Are all analyses reported? Is the sample size adequate? Has it been replicated? These questions help distinguish robust findings from potential false positives.
:::
